messages.subject: Merging namespaces
messages.body_plain:
I'm in agreement with Bob. I would be happy merging these namespaces to a single math library namespace:

    stan::math

Any objections?

[From: "Higher-Order Namespace Issues with Distributions"]

[cc-ing stan-dev list;  I just gave you (Ben) posting permission]

Ben:

What are you interested in doing?  We can use help on both
modeling and C++ coding:

  modeling:  bring existing examples up to best practices for modeling and coding
             add new examples in your area of expertise

  C++ coding:  always more functions to implement
               always more doc to write --- we want API doc throughout
               always more tests to be added
               always outstanding issues to debug

  Interface & ShinyStan coding:  I'm not sure what's needed there

I'd say starting simple is the way to go then you can work up to something
more ambitious if you're interested in more substantial contributions.  You
can look through our outstanding issues and see if there's anything you want
to tackle.

We have a meeting every Tuesday (I think they're going to move to
11 AM and maybe even move to Wednesday --- not sure).  That's a mix
of modeling (or whatever else Andrew or Michael are thinking about) and
software.

- Bob

messages.subject: Want to fit mixture of multivariate normals; maybe Ben and Marcus have some thoughts on this one
messages.subject_clean: Want to fit mixture of multivariate normals; maybe Ben and Marcus have some thoughts on this one
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  I was talking with Sebastian about fitting mixture of multivariate normals—it comes up for our hierarchical EP algorithm.  Basically what we’re looking for is a little program that automatically does this, probably an R function that calls Stan.  Here are the two challenges:
1.  Avoiding degenerate solutions where one mixture component has zero variance.
2.  Handling the aliasing, which requires identifying which mixture is which.

My idea is as follows:

1.  Using a default weakly informative prior that constrains the relative values of the variances.  I’m not sure how best to do this.  A fairly lightweight (from a statistical perspective) approach would be to put a prior on the determinants of the cov matrix, but I’m not sure how to easily do this in Stan so that it wouldn’t be computationally expensive.  Another approach would be to use one of our existing models such as inv-Wishart or LKJ with some hyperparameter that itself has a proper prior.  Really there are three concerns here:  first is the very basic issue of the prior constraining things to be away from the boundary; second is, if we are using a hierarchical model here, this could improve the fit by regularizing the cov matrices (under the reasonable assumption that they’re likely to be of comparable scale; third is that we want the whole thing to run fast so we want to avoid models that are expensive to evaluate.

2.  How to handle the aliasing?  In 1-d it’s simple enough because you can just constrain the means of the mixture components to be ordered:  mU_1 < mu_2 < mu_3 etc.  We could do the same in higher dimensions, using for example the first dimension and constraining those means to be increasing—but this could cause problems, for example, if there are 2 components whose means are close in dimension 1 but far apart in dimension 2.  So here’s another idea:  We first attempt to locate the K components using some crude algorithm such as nearest neighbor, so that we get K points in D-dimensional space.  We then identify the model based on the distance of the modes from these points.  I’m still not exactly sure how to do this:  if K=2 it’s easy, we could just constrain the two modes based on the difference of the distances between the 2 points.  (Actually, I’m not sure if it’s so easy to apply that constraint in Stan.)  In higher dimensions it would be easier to use a soft constraint that penalizes each mode based on its distance from the crude mode.  But that’s kinda sloppy because then we’re using the data twice and not quite fitting the model we want to fit.

The other issue is that we’d like the program to do full Bayes or optimize.  I’m hoping that running stan on optimize setting will be easier in the new rstan that’s coming soon?  I don’t like that “optimizing” function; I’d rather either call stan() with an optimize=TRUE setting or have a function called stan_optimize().  Also I would like the optimization to work with the stan() function that we have at that web-location, the version that has the make-like behavior.

Anyway, if we’re optimizing, things are simpler.  We still have to deal with issue 1 above, but issue 2 is less of a concern because we can just pick any starting point and then it should find one of the modes.

See you
A

messages.subject: (re)designing OperandsAndPartials and VectorView
messages.body_plain:
Rob and I pored over the existing designs yesterday and I
think there are a couple problems that stem from trying to
overload a single implementation to do different things rather
than writing separate implementations.

VectorView
----------

The functionality for arrays and matrices needs to be split
out so it can all live in the right place --- as is, it's
all in math/prim/meta/scal.

Do we really need to break meta out?  Should it have its own
namespace, or just go into math?  I think no and go into math.

This is a facade that unifies scalars, arrays, row vectors,
vectors, and matrices (though I'm not sure the latter makes sense).
It provides an operator[](int) implementation that returns a
T.

I'm not sure why it has a template parameter for is_vector_like.
This info is statically derivable from the template parameter T for
the wrapped type.

I'm also not sure why there's a throw_if_accessed.  I'd think
if we want something to throw when accessed, we should give it
a different specialization for type T.

Next up, I think the way forward is to generalize so that the
contained type isn't necessarily scalar.  It needs to be another
parameter S and then the critical interface is this one:

  template <typename T, typename S>
  VectorView<T, S> {
    const S operator[](int x);
  }

The current usage is for these instantiations, with U being
either a double or var or fvar<var> or fvar<fvar<var> >.

  VectorView<U, U>
  VectorView<vector<U>, U>
  VectorView<Matrix<U, R, C>, U>

and if we need an auto-throw, then something like this:

  VectorView<nil, U>

I think there should be three specialized implementations, not
just one with a conditional in the operator[]() implementation.

Then when we want to vectorize the multivariate stuff, we're
going to use things like sequences of vectors:

  VectorView<Matrix<U, Dynamic, 1>, Matrix<U, Dynamic, 1> >
  VectorView<vector<Matrix<U, Dynamic, 1>, Matrix<U, Dynamic, 1> >

and similarly for sequences of matrices.  We only have two constructors
because you can't make a matrix of matrices (well you could, but Stan
doesn't require it, so we shouldn't bother coding it).

OperandsAndPartials
--------------------

I think the main issue here is that we want to split it into
several implementations.  At the very least, I'd think we'd want an
fvar, var, and double version, though maybe var and double could
be combined?

Ideally it could be generalized to allow not just scalars to
be wrapped for derivatives, but also vectors and matrices.  These
should all behave in exactly the same way (use the viewed interface
to update derivatives, with adding happening if they are broadcast).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, May 7, 2015 at 9:38:59 AM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Here are the two challenges:
> 1.  Avoiding degenerate solutions where one mixture component has zero variance.

We need to be more specific about communicating this problem to users. It is pretty easy to ensure that a marginal variance is positive. The main difficulty is conditional variances going to zero, particularly when optimizing.

>
> 1.  Using a default weakly informative prior that constrains the relative values of the variances.  I’m not sure how best to do this.  A fairly lightweight (from a statistical perspective) approach would be to put a prior on the determinants of the cov matrix, but I’m not sure how to easily do this in Stan so that it wouldn’t be computationally expensive.

Anything parameterized with (large) covariance matrices is expensive (and not so accurate numerically). Anything parameterized with Cholesky factors is cheap and pretty accurate. That includes (log) determinants.

> Another approach would be to use one of our existing models such as inv-Wishart or LKJ with some hyperparameter that itself has a proper prior.

I think you want to avoid putting infinite density on singular matrices. This is kind of hard to do numerically with the inverse Wishart because the determinant term and the trace term pull in different directions as the covariance matrix approaches being singular. For LKJ it is simply a matter of constraining the shape parameter to be > 1. Also, the decomposition into standard deviations and a correlation matrix makes it easier to deal with the ordering below.

> 2.  How to handle the aliasing?  In 1-d it’s simple enough because you can just constrain the means of the mixture components to be ordered:  mU_1 < mu_2 < mu_3 etc.  We could do the same in higher dimensions, using for example the first dimension and constraining those means to be increasing—but this could cause problems, for example, if there are 2 components whose means are close in dimension 1 but far apart in dimension 2.

It could be subject to the same problems, but I would try constraining the standard deviations to be increasing over the mixture components. You could do this for one variable or compose the standard deviations for each mixture as a simplex multiplied by a scale parameter and make the scale parameters to be a pos_ordered vector.

> The other issue is that we’d like the program to do full Bayes or optimize.  I’m hoping that running stan on optimize setting will be easier in the new rstan that’s coming soon?  I don’t like that “optimizing” function; I’d rather either call stan() with an optimize=TRUE setting or have a function called stan_optimize().  Also I would like the optimization to work with the stan() function that we have at that web-location, the version that has the make-like behavior.

They take different settings, so it is a bit harder to add a optimize argument to stan(). But if having an alias for optimize() called stan_optimize() is worth enough for you to answer user's questions as to which one to use, I'll put it in.

> Anyway, if we’re optimizing, things are simpler.  We still have to deal with issue 1 above, but issue 2 is less of a concern because we can just pick any starting point and then it should find one of the modes.

In sense that issue 2 is less of a problem, yes. But issue 1 is less simple under optimization because the optimum can correspond to a singular covariance matrix.

Ben

messages.subject: suggestion regarding error messages
messages.body_plain:
Hi, often when I run Stan I get this error message:

—

Error in rstan::sflist2stanfit(out) :
  The following elements of ‘sflist' do not contain samples: 1, 2, 3, 4.

—

And it’s hard for me to figure out what this means.  Often this is a signal that I’ve forgot to specify something in the data, or that some of the data objects in R are the wrong size or the wrong shape or have missingness.  In this case it turned out there was a problem in the model where I’d screwed up on an index for a matrix and was looking for an element that wasn’t there (it was a 50x13 matrix and I was looking for something with first index 51).  So if it’s possible to make this error message more specific it could be helpful, as I see it a lot and it can be hard to find.  (This one took me 1/2 hour to debug.)

Thx
A

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
What we want is someone to take a pass over all the
models and make sure they're up to our current thinking
in terms of priors, coding efficiency, and coding style.

We'd ideally like to have for each BUGS model:

  1) direct translation of the BUGS models, preserving priors

  2) model with our preferred priors

So while they're mostly there, they're in various stages
of having both versions for each model and (2) being up to our
current coding practices (vectorization, priors, etc.)

For example, the very first example in the vol1 needs to be
updated:

https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/tree/master/bugs_examples/vol1/blocker

I'm assuming this is a reasonable direct translation (though maybe using the regular
binomial instead of binomial-logit would be more faithful, we're more concerned
about having the same model than the same coding, so algebraic differences like
binomial(inv_logit(alpha)) vs. binomial_logit(alpha) shouldn't matter).

What we want is a "best practices" version with weakly informative priors as
recommended in the regression chapter of the manual.

We'd also love to get simulations going for all these models, but that's
a secondary concern.

For the ARM models, they all need to be tested --- I think many of them
are broken.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Translation of examples in Hill, Gelman books into Stan code
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Translation of examples in Hill, Gelman books into Stan code
messages.body_plain:
I’d actually argue that simulations are paramount!

Recall that we have two problems: is our fit parsimonious with the
given model and is our model parsimonious with the “truth”?
Simulated data and our diagnostics checks the former, PPCs
check the latter.

I think it’d be great if for every example we had:

Step 1:
Simulate data from the model
Fit the model to the simulated data
Check diagnostics (n_divergent is zero for all iterations, tree_depth < max_depth for all iterations, R_hat < 1.1)
  — if diagnostics fail improve model with a note explaining the fix
Check fit to exact results
  — if fit is poor then improve model with a note explaining the fix

Step 2:
Fit the model to the true data
Check diagnostics (n_divergent is zero for all iterations, tree_depth < max_depth for all iterations, R_hat < 1.1)
  — if diagnostics fail improve model with a note explaining the fix
Check posterior predictive checks
  — if PPCs are bad improve model with a note explaining the fix

Basically, we want to encourage people to always see if they can recover the results from
simulated data before moving on to evaluating their model with PPCs.

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have started to have a go at looking at the Stan translation of the BUGS example 1 (https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/tree/master/bugs_examples/vol1/blocker), that is in the repository. I have tried to follow Bob's list of example points (https://github.com/stan-dev/example-models/blob/master/README.md), by first simulating data from the model, and fitting the model to the fake data, then checking the diagnostics. Two  of the checks appear ok: the value of Rhat < 1.1 for all parameters, and tree_depth<max_depth for all iterations. However, for the "n_divergent" parameter, I find that for about 10/2000 iterations this parameter is 1.

Forgive me; this is probably due to my misunderstanding of the problem. I understand from reading the literature that this parameter indicates that the integrator is diverging during warm up (the first 1000 iterations). I have tried various re-parameterisations, as well as changing the priors (I have changed the scale parameter to be a cauchy(0,2.5) and tried using a normal rather than t prior for delta). I have also tried manually specifying a stepsize, to prevent the integrator stepping too far, but I cannot seem to prevent this divergence from occurring.

Looking at the indices where the divergence occurs, it appears to happen frequently at iterations around: 2, 3, 4, 9, 102, 152, 252, 452, 952.

I attach the RStan script file, which first generates simulated data, then fits the model to the simulated data. I also attach the Stan file, which has only been changed a bit vs the version on git. A finally attach the real data file.

Any hints/tips would be most welcome. As I have said, I am not an expert at HMC!

Best,

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Firstly, divergences during warmup are ignorable as they usually typically
denote poor steps in the adaptation instead of pathologies in the sampler.
So if the divergences are really occurring only in the first 1000 iterations
then you’re fine.

It’s only when you see divergences in the sampling phase that you have
to worry.  In this case manually specifying a step size will not be sufficient
because the adaptation will rapidly change the initial value (although
setting a lower step size can sometimes speed up adaptation if larger
step sizes lead to awkward parameter values and expensive likelihood
computations).  What you have to do is increase the target acceptance
probability (change “delta” parameter from the default 0.8 to 0.9 or
higher as necessary for removing the divergences).

For more see http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] transforms...
messages.body_plain:
That's a good question.  The correlation transform is just
a scaled and shifted inverse logit

  2 * inv_logit(x) - 1

We could scale x if we think 20's not going to be enough.
But I don't think anyone's going to be initializating
at (-20,20) or beyond.

The transform does bound how close rho will be able to
get to -1 or 1.  But inv_logit(20) is pretty close to 1,
so it's probably not an issue if people stay away from
super high or low correlations (which are usually problematic
for other reasons).

I think there's a whole lot of research that could be done
on which transforms are more efficient.  For instance, they could
be largely linear within their main range and then highly curved
at the edges.  We could also do that with just the log transform
for the lower-bound or upper-bound constraints.  For example,

  (0,inf) -> (-inf, inf)

by taking this piece to be linear

  (0.01,inf) -> (0.01,inf)

and then using a non-linear transform here that's
smooth at the boundary

  (0, 0.01) -> (-inf, 0.01)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] transforms...
messages.body_plain:
Piecewise is always dangerous.  I think the real issue
is that the argument to the logistic is unscaled.  If you
really do have large arguments then you’d want to
do something like inv_logit(alpha * x) such that
alpha * x ~ O(1).  This carries over to other transforms,
and theoretically we could have tunable transforms.
But the better answer is to invoke the Folk Theorem
and tell people to rescale their data and parameters
to O(1) as this alleviates all the other numerical
problems, too.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
messages.body_plain:
Had a chance to talk to Tom — we’ll spend plenty more time talking over
the next few days.  Firstly, the code in Tom’s repo should be up to date
with the current implementation.  What’s great is that CVODE could be
called from the C++ with a simple extern which bodes well for integration.
He also finite-differenced the autodiff gradients to approximate the Hessian
to compute the Jacobian instead of letting CVODE compute it implicitly.
It might be worth using the block-diagonal approximation to test integration
without having to wait for the higher-order autodiff.

There seem to be some stability issues but hopefully we can figure that
out when we work through the implementation.

messages.body_plain:
I have questions, then things I think we should do before we get it into the code base.

Questions:
1) Is the branch on your fork the latest version?
2) Could we move that to the main repo (github.com/stan-dev/stan <http://github.com/stan-dev/stan>)? I'd be happy to give you permissions to the main repo (if you don't already).
3) Have you dealt with conditional builds? I haven't thought too much about it, but we definitely want Stan to build even without having installed CVODE.

Things we need to do:
1) tests: unit tests, tests to make sure all generated ODEs work
2) doc: at the class level, in the documentation
3) evaluations: how do the different solvers (within and outside of CVODE) compare. Does it actually do a reasonable job with a stiff solver on a non-stiff problem? Should we be looking at ARKode or LSODA instead?

Daniel

> I have questions, then things I think we should do before we get it

It is my latest/final version, but it is based on an older version of

stan/rstan. Since the big refactoring of the stan code, things seem to
have moved around quite a bit.

> 2) Could we move that to the main repo (github.com/stan-dev/stan <http://github.com/stan-dev/stan>)? I'd
> be happy to give you permissions to the main repo (if you don't
> already).
>

I could do that. I don't know how to deal with the dependence on an old
version of rstan however.

> 3) Have you dealt with conditional builds? I haven't thought too much
> about it, but we definitely want Stan to build even without having
> installed CVODE.
>

I have done this many times and it's easy to do. Not sure how to do it
in the stan build system however. If this is not available in the
current build system, I'm afraid you'll need to add this feature. I
usually work with autotools or cmake.
>
>

> Things we need to do:
>
> 1) tests: unit tests, tests to make sure all generated ODEs work
>

Since my implementation is a drop-in replacement for the existing
solver, I'm just using the existing unit tests. I did need to change
some of the thresholds as I'm asking for such an accurate solution from
CVODE that the tests fail because the FD gradients are not good as a
reference. This was all checked in matlab with the true analytic
solutions. Maybe it's a good idea to add this as a unit test as well,
using the true analytic solution as a reference instead of the FD
estimate.

> 2) doc: at the class level, in the documentation
>

The CVODE implementation is a drop-in replacement, so I kept the
available documentation. I can surely add more documentation wherever
needed.

> 3) evaluations: how do the different solvers (within and outside of
> CVODE) compare. Does it actually do a reasonable job with a stiff
> solver on a non-stiff problem? Should we be looking at ARKode or LSODA
> instead?
>
>

The underlying algorithms in CVODE are the same as LSODA ((BDF and
Adams-Moulton). I haven't looked at the LSODA implementation, but I
suspect that it might have some small numerical differences. An
interesting aspect of LSODA is that it has heuristics builtin to switch
automatically between the explicit and implicit methods. Comparisons are
great, but I fear the results might be too problem-specific to
generalize. I would maybe even advocate the ability for the user to
decide on the method used (as well as absolute and relative tolerances!
). Using the simulation mode in stan, the user can investigate which
method gives the best trade-off.

Tom

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Tom. All great points. More inline.

On Thu, May 21, 2015 at 10:27 AM, Tom Haber <tom....@uhasselt.be> wrote:

> On Thu, 2015-05-21 at 09:58 -0400, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > I have questions, then things I think we should do before we get it
> > into the code base.
> >
> >
> > Questions:
> >
> > 1) Is the branch on your fork the latest version?
> >

> It is my latest/final version, but it is based on an older version of
> stan/rstan. Since the big refactoring of the stan code, things seem to
> have moved around quite a bit.

Ok; good to know that's the final version.

Yes, things have moved, but it's still tractable.

>
> > 2) Could we move that to the main repo (github.com/stan-dev/stan <http://github.com/stan-dev/stan>)? I'd
> > be happy to give you permissions to the main repo (if you don't
> > already).
> >

> I could do that. I don't know how to deal with the dependence on an old
> version of rstan however.

Ok. I'll let you know when it's on a branch in Stan. I don't see the connection to RStan?

>
> > 3) Have you dealt with conditional builds? I haven't thought too much
> > about it, but we definitely want Stan to build even without having
> > installed CVODE.
> >

> I have done this many times and it's easy to do. Not sure how to do it
> in the stan build system however. If this is not available in the
> current build system, I'm afraid you'll need to add this feature. I
> usually work with autotools or cmake.

We don't have it in yet and we don't use autotools or cmake. Do you know the mechanism that does it? C macros? Something else? The problem is that CVODE doesn't include enough headers to compile unless you run their install instructions. That means a user needs to install to make all of Stan compile. That isn't what we want.

> > Things we need to do:
> >
> > 1) tests: unit tests, tests to make sure all generated ODEs work
> >

> Since my implementation is a drop-in replacement for the existing
> solver, I'm just using the existing unit tests. I did need to change
> some of the thresholds as I'm asking for such an accurate solution from
> CVODE that the tests fail because the FD gradients are not good as a
> reference. This was all checked in matlab with the true analytic
> solutions. Maybe it's a good idea to add this as a unit test as well,
> using the true analytic solution as a reference instead of the FD
> estimate.

Yes, that would be great to add those as unit tests as well.

>
> > 2) doc: at the class level, in the documentation
> >

> The CVODE implementation is a drop-in replacement, so I kept the
> available documentation. I can surely add more documentation wherever
> needed.

Thanks. Let's start by moving things and we'll take inventory later.

>
> > 3) evaluations: how do the different solvers (within and outside of
> > CVODE) compare. Does it actually do a reasonable job with a stiff
> > solver on a non-stiff problem? Should we be looking at ARKode or LSODA
> > instead?
> >
> >

> The underlying algorithms in CVODE are the same as LSODA ((BDF and
> Adams-Moulton). I haven't looked at the LSODA implementation, but I
> suspect that it might have some small numerical differences. An
> interesting aspect of LSODA is that it has heuristics builtin to switch
> automatically between the explicit and implicit methods. Comparisons are
> great, but I fear the results might be too problem-specific to
> generalize. I would maybe even advocate the ability for the user to
> decide on the method used (as well as absolute and relative tolerances!
> ). Using the simulation mode in stan, the user can investigate which
> method gives the best trade-off.

Thanks for the info. I didn't realize it was using a heuristic to go between the two.

parser and code generator and user-facing interface and thus doc.  And the
more permutations there are, the more work it is now and to maintain going
forward.

Hi!

The new ODE solver is shaping up, which is great! As most users will be using this in the context of hierarchical models, it would make sense to consider adding some mechanism which allows for embarassingly parallelism, i.e. evaluate the ODE for N patients in parallel and since due to the need for sensitivities and oftentimes many patients, this can be a very worthwhile thing todo. Of course, this would be beneficial in general, not only for ODE type models, but all hierarchical models with expensive model function evaluation.

Maybe this can be done with some type of openMP type statements? No idea, just a thought.

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: proposal draft for RStan interface
messages.body_plain:
Ahead of working on the Python/R under-the-hood refactor when
Allen gets here, I tried to go through the current R interface and
whittle things down (and expand a bit) to where I think it should go.
I'd think that roughly the same interface would work in Python.

I hope this is close enough to idiomatic for R that it's not
too embarrassing --- but please send feedback (up to and including
telling me I should just stay out of R!).

The biggest change is simplifying what functions do and where some
of the action is, as well as splitting some of the functions out (like
stan() is now stan_nuts, stan_hmc, and stan_diagnose).

I don't think this loses any functionality other than the big fit
object, which I don't think we should have.  And it's assuming some
functionality we don't yet have, like being able to input a mass matrix.

I can move this over to a wiki (on RStan or Stan's repo?) if people
think that'll be easier and the response isn't to just get out of the
way of RStan.

- Bob

1.  Compilation
------------------------------------------------------------
The compilation function compiles a Stan program to a dynamic shared
object (DSO) and optionally saves it.

compiled_program
rtan::stan_compile(                # DEFAULTS
  source = (<string> || <path>)    # no default
  name = <string>,                 # empty
  boost = <path>,                  # use BH
  eigen = <path>,                  # use RcppEigen
  opt = ("fast" || "debug"),       # "fast"
  save_dso = <bool>,               # FALSE
  debug_code = <bool>              # TRUE
);

* Is there any reason to keep the name option?
* How long-lived is the "save_dso" option?
    - Where is it saved?
* If we allow optimize settings, is there a way to have it scope
  over just the call and not affect the R global build environment?
* Is there a way we can have make-like behavior here where if there's
  a saved version and the model file or code have not changed, don't
  do anything?
* Do we need the other existing compiler options ("presentation1",
  "presentation2", and "small")?
* Should the save_dso provide a path rather than a boolean?
* Is it possible to save the DSO across sessions?
* Should the dave_dso defalt be true and if so, use temp?
* Do we ever need NDEBUG=false?  That is, shouldn't we just always
  have -DNDEBUG set to turn off debugging?  (The double-negative

compiled_program
--------------------
This should only include the compiled Stan program and methods
to do variable conversion, extract names, compute log densities, etc.

Slots:
  name : <string>
  stan_code : <string>
  cpp_code  : <string>
  dso : <S4 cxxdso>  (from inline)
  cxx_flags: <string>
Methods:
  double
  log_prob(
    unconstrained_params = <vector>,
    jacobian = <bool>);

  list(value=<double>, grad=<vector>)
  log_prob_grad(
    unconstrained_params = <vector>,
    jacobian = <bool>);

      return$value : <double>
      return$grad : <vector>

  list(
  constrain_params(
    unconstrained_params = <vector>);

  vector
  constrain_params_vec(
    unconstrained_params = <vector>);

  vector
  unconstrain_params(
    params = (<list> || vector));

* Seems there should be a better way to organize this, but I
  can't see it.  And maybe some shorter names

2. NUTS
------------------------------------------------------------

mcmc_fit
rstan::stan_nuts(
  program = <compiled_program>,       # no default
  data = (<list> || <environment>),   # top-level environment by default
  max_treedepth = <int>,              # 10
  chain_ids = <ints>,                 # 1:4
  num_warmup = <int>,                 # 10
  num_samples = <int>,                # 10
  init=(<double>                      # 2.0
        || <list>
        || <list of lists>
        || <function>)
  stepsize=<double>,                  # 1.0
  metric = ("unit_e",                 # "diag_e"
           || "diag_e"
           || "dense_e"
           || <vector>
           || <matrix>),
  adapt_stepsize = <bool>,            # TRUE
  adapt_mass_matrix = <bool>,         # TRUE
  adapt = list(gamma=<double>,
               kappa=<double>,
               t0=<double>,
               init_buffer=<int>,
               term_buffer=<int>,
               adapt_window=<int>)    # ...
  params_to_save = (NA
                   || <vector(char)>) # NA
  save_warmup = <bool>,               # TRUE
  thin = <int>,                       # 1
  sample_file = <path>,               # NA
  diagnostic_file = <path>,           # NA
  refresh = <int>,                    # 1
  verbose = ("quiet"
             || "standard"
             || "verbose"),           # standard
  seed = <int>                        # random from R
)

* Return value just includes the result in such a way that it
  can be extracted as before.
* Return value won't include the compiled program (or source).
* Should return value include timing information?
* There's no append_samples = <bool>
* There's no option to compile the model from within the stan_nuts
  call.
* data defaults to top-level environment with lazy read (not how
  it's done now);  list is list of values as before
* Instead of "chains" and a start ID, there's just a "chain_ids"
  argument supplying both the chains and the ID, defaulting to the usual
* Default num_warmup and num_samples very small by default (but shouldn't
  be so small as to trigger scary messages about adaptation)
* Metric is specified by name of type or by value;  the names default
  to unit values for init
* Those adapt parameters are all for adapt_stepsize, right?
* Are there adaptation parameters for mass_matrix, like regularization?
* params_to_save defaults to NA (or all), or a positive list of whole
  parameter names.
* sample_file gets a copy of the output written to it, but return
  object still created --- should this just move so that the return
  object has a save on it?  Or should setting this cause the return of
  this function to be NA?

mcmc_fit
--------------------

3. EHMC
------------------------------------------------------------
Plain old HMC looks just like NUTS, but with max_treedepth replaced
by integration time:

mcmc_fit
rstan::stan_hmc(...
  int_time = <double>
  ...
)

4. Optimize
------------------------------------------------------------

optimization_fit
stan_lbfgs(
  program = <compiled_program>,
  data = (<list> || <environment>),
  init = (<double>
          || <list>
          || <list of lists>
          || <function>),
  optimization_file = <file>,
  verbose = ("quiet" || "verbose"),
  hessian = <bool>,                       # FALSE
  max_iterations = <int>,                 # NA
  save_iterations = <bool>,               # FALSE
  refresh = <int>,                        # 5
  init_alpha = <double>,                  # ???
  tol_obj = <double>,
  tol_grad = <double>,
  tol_param = <double>,
  tol_obj_rel = <double>,
  tol_grad_rel = <double>,
  tol_param_rel = <double>,
  seed = <int>
)

* Should verbose be a boolean?
* What does current as_vector do? Current doc says "flag indicating whether a
  vector is used to for the point estimate found. A list can be
  used instead by specifying it to be FALSE"
* What's the behavior of tolerances if more than one's specified?  I'd
  think it should be read as AND or as OR.
* No option to specify parameter return as vector --- use a compiled
  model's conversion.

optimization_fit
--------------------
    $par : parameters (as list)
    $value : lp__

5. Diagnose
------------------------------------------------------------

diagnostics
rstan::stan_diagnose(
  program = <compiled_program>,
  data = (<list> || <environment>),
  init = (<double>
          || <list>
          || <list of lists>
          || <function>),
  epsilon = <double>,
  error_threshold = <double>,
  seed = <int>,
  chain_ids = <int>)

* arguments just a subset of those for NUTS/HMC
* returns diagnostics for each of the chain_ids
* not sure what goes in diagnostics as long as it's
  easy to print

diagnostics
--------------------
?? not sure what should go in here --- it needs to be printable

messages.subject: <cmath> and std:: vs. <math.h> and ::
messages.body_plain:
[moved off issue, changed subject]

The original question is why so many "using std::log" and
whatnot in the code now?

We're moving to consistently using <cmath>, the C++
math library where the functions are declared in the
standard library (std::) namespace.  <math.h> is the C version
and brings in functions in the top-level (::) namespace.  Thus
the <math.h> versions are always in scope because the symbols
from a containing namespace area always available in nested
namespaces.  So anything defined in stan:: would be visible
in stan::math, for example.

It's better not to bring namespaces in wholesale to gain
more control on what might get called.

- Bob

messages.subject: exact reproducibility in rstan with parallelization
messages.subject_clean: exact reproducibility in rstan with parallelization
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I saw that the new rstan seems to include parallelization which is great. Since not yet rolled out, I would like to suggest the following for consideration:

- Exact reproducibility (ER) is quite important in some applications and it would be great if the parallelization feature in rstan maintains ER even if the users switches from sequential to parallel executing (and of course exact results should not matter on the number of cpus).

- One strategy would be to initialize things in the main process and then pass the final inits to the childs (assuming that a R function has been supplied as init)

- If ER is decided not to be important in this case, then it would be great if the user is given the possibility to handle it himself.

- I noticed the use of mclapply which has a subtle behavior in general. That is, if I make a stan fit two times in a row with it, I will end up getting two times exactly the same result - *without* any set.seed call in between. Example

fit1 <- stan(..., parallel=TRUE)
fit2 <- stan(..., parallel=TRUE)

This is contradictory in that I always expect the internal R random number generator to be in a different state once I call a stochastic function. The reason is that mclapply is quite brutal in the sense that it resets the R random stream. Not nice, but users could be warned or you make sure to always draw at least 1 random number not in the child processes.

Just my two cents concerning ER...

Best,
Sebastian

Is there a case where you don't get reproducibility and you set
the seed and chain_id?

I'm not sure if the parallelization will land in a near-future
RStan because of issues with platforms and stability.  We're going to
back off on features if necessary in order to get more stability.

In which case, reproducibility will be the responsibility of the caller
and we just have to make sure it does the right thing given a seed
and chain_id.

I think the R RNG is used to set the seed, but that's the expected
behavior if the parallelization happens in a different process.
I think we should be clear on what's going on, not try to tinker with
the RNG in one R process based on what goes on in another.

- Bob

> - I noticed the use of mclapply which has a subtle behavior in general. That is, if I make a stan fit two times in a row with it, I will end up getting two times exactly the same result - *without* any set.seed call in between. Example
>
> fit1 <- stan(..., parallel=TRUE)
> fit2 <- stan(..., parallel=TRUE)
>
> This is contradictory in that I always expect the internal R random number generator to be in a different state once I call a stochastic function. The reason is that mclapply is quite brutal in the sense that it resets the R random stream. Not nice, but users could be warned or you make sure to always draw at least 1 random number not in the child processes.

We aren't doing mclapply() interally; only parLapply(). It should be exactly reproduceable if you pass a seed to stan() unless you also pass an init function() that is evaluated in the child R process without any particular seed. But that can be overcome by calling your init function in the parent R process and passing the result to the init argument of stan() as a list of numeric lists.

Ben

messages.subject: feature request: elementwise matrix operations
messages.body_plain:
I'll open an issue unless this has already been discussed elsewhere.

For a matrix M, exp(M) works, but cos(M), sin(M), fabs(M), pow(M) etc.
do not. I'm trying to do a periodic GP using cos, so this would be
very helpful. I imagine there are other use cases, and of course the
work around is to just write a function/for loop.

Following exp's lead, I guess this should ideally be implemented for
row_vector and vector as well.

Note: at some point there might be a matrix product implemented, so
it's worth figuring out if pow(M) should be the elementwise one, i.e.
figure out what these will be named.

Best,
Seth

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I got the code up and running on a fairly large example:

- Installation went semi-smoothly due to the yet experimental state of things, but install-cvode worked (after a cmake install)

- My model compiled with the develop cmdstan

- It starts to run and things look promising

- ...but after 2h or so the progress appears not be faster than with the RK integrator (not 100% sure though on this speed thing) *and* memory consumption continuously increases into the GB range (while the model starts off with a few 100 MB).

It looks to me that there is a memory leak and possibly further issues. Not sure.

Looking forward to the progress here, I really hope this gets ODEs going faster.

Cheers,
Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
Concerning speed: What confused me is that you, Tom, suggest smaller tolerances which I would expect to make things slower, no?

In any case - I agree that having these fairly crucial parameters configurable by the user is indeed important.

Out of curiosity: To my knowledge cvode needs Jacobians as input - is the Stan autodiff used to get this?

I am happy to throw my example again at Stan-cvode...

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
messages.body_plain:
> On May 30, 2015, at 12:56 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Concerning speed: What confused me is that you, Tom, suggest smaller tolerances which I would expect to make things slower, no?

Tom used smaller tolerances.  When we compare speeds,
the tolerances should be the same.

I have no idea how much these tolerances matter.  We
need to experiment more.

> In any case - I agree that having these fairly crucial parameters configurable by the user is indeed important.

We can add control for tolerances as one or two more arguments
to integrate_ode.  Both absolute and relative?

Stan functions don't have optional parameters, so I'm always
reluctant to add params until we're sure we'll need them.

We could also do this through the compiler if we think we
just need to find the right global setting.  That is, they
wouldn't be part of a model, but part of how it's compiled:

  program <- stan_model(file="foo.stan", ode_tol_absolute=1e-6, ode_tol_relative=1e-6, ...);

> Out of curiosity: To my knowledge cvode needs Jacobians as input - is the Stan autodiff used to get this?

Nope --- not Stan autodiff yet --- I believe it just uses finite diffs
internally.

Michael's worked out the math so we can supply the Jacobians
with the sensitivities --- it's going to require higher-order
autodiff, though, with multiple passes per evaluation to get the
Jacobian, so it's not necessarily going to be any faster.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
messages.body_plain:
I have a model which can be a little sensitive to errors in the ODE
solution, so I made the tolerances much lower and thus slower.

The choice of the tolerances depends entirely on the model used and what
is expected from it. Like most tolerances and thresholds, it's not an
easy matter.

CVODE does require jacobians, but it has a default option to compute
them using Finite Differencing. However, in my implementation, stan's
autodiff is used to supply the jacobians to CVODE. In the sensitivities
case, you need the hessian of the ODE which I currently computed using
FD on top of autodiff. The stability needs some further investigation,
but speed-wise it is better than FD-ing a huge, very sparse matrix.

Tom

@Tom: Sounds like what you did made sense - is that how the current Stan cvode branch is setup to work? Also: Great that you already pinpointed the cvode memory issue - did you sent te patch to the cvode folks?

Best,
Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Stiff ode solver
messages.body_plain:
~/cmdstan(develop)$ grep -R "1e-6" stan/src/stan
...
stan/src/stan/math/prim/arr/functor/integrate_ode.hpp:      const double absolute_tolerance = 1e-6;
stan/src/stan/math/prim/arr/functor/integrate_ode.hpp:      const double relative_tolerance = 1e-6;

- Bob

> On May 31, 2015, at 5:16 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> @Bob: I think making these tolerances (absolute+relative) configurable just like the sampler options is the right thing to do. I think this is quite the same in the sense as it affects how the background numerics of Stan is configured and there is no need to ever adjust these tolerances during a stan run (i.e. for different parts of the data different tolerances is not needed). In the meantime - where can I set these thresholds manually, i.e. what do I need to "grep" for in the hpp files?
>
> @Tom: Sounds like what you did made sense - is that how the current Stan cvode branch is setup to work? Also: Great that you already pinpointed the cvode memory issue - did you sent te patch to the cvode folks?
>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>
> On Saturday, May 30, 2015 at 8:00:09 PM UTC+2, Tom HABER wrote:
>> I have a model which can be a little sensitive to errors in the ODE
>> solution, so I made the tolerances much lower and thus slower.
>>
>> The choice of the tolerances depends entirely on the model used and what
>> is expected from it. Like most tolerances and thresholds, it's not an
>> easy matter.
>>
>> CVODE does require jacobians, but it has a default option to compute
>> them using Finite Differencing. However, in my implementation, stan's
>> autodiff is used to supply the jacobians to CVODE. In the sensitivities
>> case, you need the hessian of the ODE which I currently computed using
>> FD on top of autodiff. The stability needs some further investigation,
>> but speed-wise it is better than FD-ing a huge, very sparse matrix.
>>
>> Tom
>>
>> On Sat, 2015-05-30 at 13:34 -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>>> On May 30, 2015, at 12:56 PM, Sebastian Weberw rote:
>>>>
>>>> Concerning speed: What confused me is that you, Tom, suggest smaller tolerances which I would expect to make things slower, no?
>>>
>>> Tom used smaller tolerances.  When we compare speeds,
>>> the tolerances should be the same.
>>>
>>> I have no idea how much these tolerances matter.  We
>>> need to experiment more.
>>>
>>>> In any case - I agree that having these fairly crucial parameters configurable by the user is indeed important.
>>>
>>> We can add control for tolerances as one or two more arguments
>>> to integrate_ode.  Both absolute and relative?
>>>
>>> Stan functions don't have optional parameters, so I'm always
>>> reluctant to add params until we're sure we'll need them.
>>>
>>> We could also do this through the compiler if we think we
>>> just need to find the right global setting.  That is, they
>>> wouldn't be part of a model, but part of how it's compiled:
>>>
>>>  program <- stan_model(file="foo.stan", ode_tol_absolute=1e-6, ode_tol_relative=1e-6, ...);
>>>
>>>> Out of curiosity: To my knowledge cvode needs Jacobians as input - is the Stan autodiff used to get this?
>>>
>>> Nope --- not Stan autodiff yet --- I believe it just uses finite diffs
>>> internally.
>>>
>>> Michael's worked out the math so we can supply the Jacobians
>>> with the sensitivities --- it's going to require higher-order
>>> autodiff, though, with multiple passes per evaluation to get the
>>> Jacobian, so it's not necessarily going to be any faster.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>
